tierWindow.goal: Build a revision strategy: organise your time and your knowledge gaps into a plan, and populate it with active techniques chosen to fit your material.
tierWindow.cognitiveDemand: Application and organisation (apply, build, select, plan), beyond the introductory understand/identify level and short of the advanced self-directed adaptation.
tierWindow.taskComplexity: Structured multi-step tasks: assembling a strategy from parts, contrasting active with passive approaches, and matching techniques to material.
tierWindow.autonomy: Moderate scaffolding; worked examples contrast a weaker and a stronger approach; the learner makes choices and plans, with guidance.

decidedValue.priorExperienceAnchor: The learner already understands what exams are and why a revision strategy is needed (the introductory tier). They are now ready to put that into action: to build a strategy and choose techniques for it, rather than only recognising that one is necessary. They have not yet mastered the self-directed application of techniques or exam-day performance (the advanced tier).

decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has three short lessons. First, the anatomy of a revision strategy: the two things it is built on. Second, active revision rather than passive review. Third, choosing active techniques from the visual, auditory and kinaesthetic families. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the three lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This course is about building a revision strategy: turning the time before an exam into a plan that works. By the end you will be able to build a strategy around your use of time and the gaps in your knowledge, apply active-learning principles rather than relying on passive review, and select revision techniques that fit your material.

You already know exams need a strategy. This is where you build one. A good strategy is not about revising for longer; it is about revising in the right way, on the right things, at the right time.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Three course outcomes framed up front: build a strategy around time and gaps, apply active-learning principles, select techniques to fit the material.

practiceConnection.academic: A revision strategy is not just something you need for exams. Planning your time against your goals, finding the gaps in what you know, and working actively rather than passively are how you manage any large piece of work. Build the strategy now and you build a way of working that carries through your degree and into professional life.

grounding.note: W-OPEN states the three course outcomes and why they matter (AL-5)

decidedValue.whereNextBody: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the advanced revising and exams course takes these active techniques further and into exam-day performance, where you apply them under timed conditions. Going wider: the same planning and active-learning habits underpin Academic Writing, Researching and Reflective Practice.
decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. A revision strategy is no longer a vague intention: it is something you can build and fill. You can name the two elements it rests on, your use of time and the gaps in your knowledge, and plan its stages. You can tell active revision from passive review and say why active works better. And you can choose techniques from the visual, auditory and kinaesthetic families to fit your material. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, a revision strategy is something you build for every module, not just once. Each time you plan your time against your gaps, choose an active technique over a passive one, and match the method to the material, you are using what this course gave you. The same habits serve any large task, in study and in work.
